Booking Holdings Launches Vayo With Planned $100 Million Investment In AI Personal Travel Agent
Booking Holdings has launched Vayo, a new AI-powered personal travel agent, and plans to invest up to $100 million as it explores a more personalized approach to trip planning and management.
Vayo is launching in private beta with a waitlist open to travelers. The planned investment depends on continued product development and market conditions. The company is designed to manage an entire trip rather than operate as a general-purpose chatbot or assistant focused on individual tasks.
Vayo can bring together existing travel reservations from a user’s inbox, organize trip details, identify missing components, and monitor prices. Because reservations are connected within a single itinerary, the platform is also designed to understand how changes to one part of a trip can affect others. For example, a flight delay could trigger warnings about a late hotel check-in or a dinner reservation that may need to be changed.
The company is part of Booking Holdings, whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable. Vayo is being designed to work across Booking Holdings brands as well as reservations made through competing travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels.
Vayo’s initial private beta will provide free, invite-only access focused primarily on frequent travelers. The company said the beta period will be used to gather feedback and refine the product before a broader rollout. Vayo will access only travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips rather than the rest of a user’s inbox.
Future product plans include direct booking capabilities, a native mobile application, collaborative trip planning with travel companions, and additional assistance once travelers are already on their trips.
Booking Holdings is positioning Vayo as an experiment in how AI can move beyond answering travel questions toward proactively managing the interconnected parts of a trip. The company believes personalized travel agents could anticipate user needs based on previous behavior, existing reservations, and trip context.
Vayo is led by CEO and co-founder Mike Fridgen. Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said the company is exploring how AI can reduce the amount of planning and coordination work that still falls on travelers.

“A trip isn’t a task, and travelers deserve more than a chatbot. With the backing of Booking Holdings, we’re building a personal travel agent that understands the entire trip, knows how you travel and never stops working for you. That’s Vayo.”
Mike Fridgen, CEO And Co-Founder Of Vayo
“Travel is one of the most complex consumer experiences, and too much of the work still falls on the traveler to manage. Vayo is exploring how AI can anticipate needs to make planning and managing a trip more seamless. I have confidence in the Vayo team and their ability to move with purpose, capitalize on early learnings and adapt at pace as they explore what the next generation of personalization in travel can look like.”

Booking Holdings Inc. (BKNG) Is Building Its Own AI Agent. Can Cash Flow Defend the Multiple?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:11 PM CDT 5 min read
Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is no longer only defending its travel marketplace from rival online agencies. It must also establish where its economics fit when artificial-intelligence agents can search for hotels and complete bookings for customers. On October 14, the company announced a planned $100 million investment in Vayo, a personal travel agent entering private beta. The proposed investment is small relative to Booking's approximately $120.73 billion equity valuation. Its significance therefore depends less on immediate earnings contribution and more on whether Booking remains the destination for travel transactions when discovery migrates elsewhere.
The Booking Engine Still Earns Its Place
In the second quarter of 2026, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG)'s room nights grew 5%, gross bookings increased 9%, and adjusted EBITDA rose 9% to approximately $2.6 billion. Adjusted EPS advanced 15%, helped by a 6% lower average share count. Management also increased its expected annual transformation savings run rate to $650 million from $550 million, with most incremental savings anticipated in 2027. These are tangible offsets to the idea that an AI intermediary can simply replace Booking overnight.
The company ranks third among the 10 best undervalued stocks to buy now according to Reddit, using Q2 hedge fund ownership. But two stocks ranked ahead of it. The more relevant puzzle is whether Booking's unusually strong profitability and cash-generation record deserves a different valuation from faster-growing platforms with potentially less exposure to travel demand.
Agentic AI Threatens the Route to the Customer
The risk is not necessarily that travelers stop staying in hotels. It is that an agent captures the customer relationship, compares offers and directs transactions to whichever supplier pays the lowest effective distribution cost. Meta's Muse launch intensified that concern in September. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is responding with Vayo and the September 29 launch of Lola, another AI-driven booking experience backed by the company. Its defenses include deeply fragmented accommodation inventory, loyalty benefits, payment infrastructure, and a growing range of connected trip services.
Nevertheless, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) still has a customer-acquisition bill. Second-quarter marketing expense rose 11%, faster than gross bookings, and mobile applications accounted for a high-50% share of room nights. Management said the direct-to-consumer share remained in the mid-60% range. The ability to retain direct traffic is important because a higher proportion of paid referrals could reduce the economics of each hotel night even if bookings continue to rise. Our recent comparison of Booking's profitability with Airbnb's faster-growing, differentiated supply shows why inventory, distribution and margins deserve to be considered together.
Seeking Alpha's data values Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) at 17.76 times trailing GAAP earnings and 15.31 times forward GAAP earnings; forward non-GAAP P/E is 15.37. That non-GAAP forward multiple is roughly 36% below the five-year average of 24.16, although only modestly above the sector median of 14.84. The consensus projects EPS growth of 14.59% in 2026, 18.41% in 2027, and 16.41% in 2028, a trajectory capable of reducing the prospective P/E over time if achieved.
Cash flow complicates that apparently favorable reading. The second-quarter earnings call reported $3.6 billion of free cash flow, and the company repurchased $7.4 billion of shares in the first half. But merchant bookings allow travelers' money to arrive before Booking pays accommodation providers or processes refunds. Consequently, operating cash flow can be supported by customer-related liabilities that are not distributable earnings. Our closer look at Booking's traveler advances and how much cash shareholders can actually keep addresses that important distinction.
The capital structure also deserves attention: $20.92 billion of debt sits against $17.21 billion of cash, representing approximately $3.71 billion of net debt. The balance sheet is not an immediate sign of distress, but the market's earnings multiple needs to be read alongside buybacks, working capital, and the future cost of defending customer acquisition.
Travel Weakness Makes the Timing Less Forgiving
The operating backdrop offers limited room for complacency. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) lowered its full-year gross-bookings growth expectation in August to high single digits from high single digits to low double digits, citing pressure on international travel, particularly linked to the Middle East conflict. On October 7, Wells Fargo reduced its target to $190 from $220, Equal Weight, citing long-haul weakness and AI risks. Cantor Fitzgerald moved to $170 from $220 on October 12, Neutral, while Morgan Stanley had initiated at Overweight with a $230 target in September, emphasizing supply scale as a competitive advantage.
Hedge fund ownership slipped to 92 from 95 between Q1 and Q2 2026, while shares sold short rose to 22.62 million from 20.15 million between August 31 and September 30, or 3.02% of float. These are positioning snapshots, not proof that investors have reached a verdict on Muse. The next evidence will come from direct booking trends, marketing efficiency, room-night growth, and whether Vayo or Lola can preserve Booking's transaction economics. For a useful contrast, why Airbnb's expansion may command a higher growth multiple examines a different kind of travel-platform exposure.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of BKNG as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. If you are looking for an AI stock that is more promising than BKNG and that has 10,000% upside potential, check out our report about this cheapest AI stock.

Booking Holdings CEO and President, Glenn Fogel On AI, Humans, and the Future of Travel
At the TIME100 AI event, leaders from across industries gathered to explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping the way we work and navigate an increasingly technology-driven world. Among them was Glenn Fogel, Chief Executive Officer and President of Booking Holdings, who offered a perspective grounded in one of the most universal human experiences: travel.
For Fogel, AI’s potential is not simply about making it easier to book a flight or hotel. It is about fundamentally changing the experience of planning a trip, and making travel more predictable and responsive. While people love to travel, he noted, the process of getting there can still be frustratingly complex. The challenge is often less about the trip itself than the uncertainty surrounding it: What happens when plans change?
AI, he suggested, could help address those pain points by anticipating what travelers need before they ask. Rather than simply responding to a search, an AI-powered travel experience could predict disruptions and adapt an itinerary in real time. If rain is forecast during a planned canal ride in Amsterdam, for example, AI could suggest moving the activity to a better day and finding another experience in its place.
That vision reflects a broader shift in how AI could interact with consumers: not simply responding to requests, but anticipating needs before they arise.
But Fogel also acknowledged that technological progress comes with responsibilities. The pace of AI-driven change, he said, raises important questions about how societies and economies will adapt. While AI promises meaningful advances, its broader effects—including potential disruption to jobs and communities—must remain part of the conversation.
At TIME100 AI, Fogel explored both sides of that equation: the opportunity to make travel more seamless and intuitive, and the responsibility to navigate an accelerating technological transition thoughtfully.

The ABR suggests buying Booking Holdings, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.
Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.
This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. What Could Lift Booking Holdings Stock?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:02 AM CDT 4 min read
Shares of Booking Holdings (BKNG) have lost 17.2% over the past year, lagging the S&P 500 and its 17.4% return. Following that decline, the stock trades at 17.3 times earnings. That multiple sits below the company's average of 28.3 over its last 12 fiscal quarter ends. A lower P/E means paying less for each dollar of profit, but that discount only pays off if the profit keeps growing. So what would have to go right for Booking Holdings stock to climb from here?
Booking Holdings Would Gain Most From Selling More Travel
Selling more travel would generate most of the stock's potential gain. Under Trefis's three-year scenario, higher revenue accounts for 82.4% of the upside. That means more room nights, the nights travelers book through platforms like Booking.com, alongside more flight and attraction tickets. Following these assumptions, the stock would appreciate about 49% in three years, excluding dividends.
The table compares Booking Holdings today against the scenario three years out.
An expanding multiple provides a further 28.4% of the upside, assuming a higher P/E, while a lower margin takes 10.8% back. This scenario lifts the P/E from 17.3 to 19.4. Even after that increase, the multiple would remain below the stock's own 12-quarter average of 28.3.
Where Booking Holdings' Sales Growth Comes From
The scenario models revenue growth of 11.6% a year. That pace falls slightly behind the 12.9% Booking Holdings delivered over the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. Growth slowed in the latest quarter, so the scenario needs the pace to pick up again as travelers book more nights and more of the rest of their trips through the company's sites. Room nights increased 5% and revenue rose 8% in fiscal Q2 2026, management said on the August 4, 2026 call. Executives issued a slower guide for the following period, forecasting fiscal Q3 2026 revenue growth of 4% to 6%. However, that guidance covers a single quarter rather than three years, and it assumes the conflict in the Middle East keeps weighing on long-haul travel.
Booking Holdings is also capturing more business from its most loyal customers. Members of its Genius levels 2 and 3 accounted for more than 30% of active customers in fiscal Q2 2026, representing an increase from a year earlier. Management also said that trips combining several bookings grew more than twice as fast as total transactions at Booking.com.
How Booking Holdings' Upside Changes Under Other Scenarios
Each row below alters one assumption while keeping the other two from the scenario.
Revenue growth of 9.6% a year instead of 11.6%
Net margin of 21.9% in year three instead of 24.4%
P/E of 17.3 in year three instead of 19.4
5 years at the same assumptions instead of 3
The scenario already trims the net margin, because Booking Holdings currently operates at a margin above its average for the twelve quarter ends from fiscal Q2 2023 to fiscal Q1 2026. That lower margin gives back about a tenth of the gain.
Holding the stock for three years would return nothing under these assumptions if revenue shrank 2.3% a year, against the 12.9% growth Booking Holdings delivered in the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. The investment would also return nothing if the net margin fell to 16.4% in year three, compared to 25.5% over those twelve months. The same holds true if the P/E dropped to 13.0, against 17.3 today.
Growth in room nights is the measure to watch in the company's fiscal Q3 2026 report, expected on or around November 3, 2026.

Not necessarily on Booking Holdings alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is no longer only defending its travel marketplace from rival online agencies. It must also establish where its economics fit when artificial-intelligence agents can search for hotels and complete bookings for customers. On October 14, the company announced a planned $100 million investment in Vayo, a personal travel agent entering private beta. The proposed investment is small relative to Booking's approximately $120.73 billion equity valuation. Its significance therefore depends less on immediate earnings contribution and more on whether Booking remains the destination for travel transactions when discovery migrates elsewhere.
The Booking Engine Still Earns Its Place
In the second quarter of 2026, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG)'s room nights grew 5%, gross bookings increased 9%, and adjusted EBITDA rose 9% to approximately $2.6 billion. Adjusted EPS advanced 15%, helped by a 6% lower average share count. Management also increased its expected annual transformation savings run rate to $650 million from $550 million, with most incremental savings anticipated in 2027. These are tangible offsets to the idea that an AI intermediary can simply replace Booking overnight.
The company ranks third among the 10 best undervalued stocks to buy now according to Reddit, using Q2 hedge fund ownership. But two stocks ranked ahead of it. The more relevant puzzle is whether Booking's unusually strong profitability and cash-generation record deserves a different valuation from faster-growing platforms with potentially less exposure to travel demand.
Agentic AI Threatens the Route to the Customer
The risk is not necessarily that travelers stop staying in hotels. It is that an agent captures the customer relationship, compares offers and directs transactions to whichever supplier pays the lowest effective distribution cost. Meta's Muse launch intensified that concern in September. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is responding with Vayo and the September 29 launch of Lola, another AI-driven booking experience backed by the company. Its defenses include deeply fragmented accommodation inventory, loyalty benefits, payment infrastructure, and a growing range of connected trip services.
Nevertheless, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) still has a customer-acquisition bill. Second-quarter marketing expense rose 11%, faster than gross bookings, and mobile applications accounted for a high-50% share of room nights. Management said the direct-to-consumer share remained in the mid-60% range. The ability to retain direct traffic is important because a higher proportion of paid referrals could reduce the economics of each hotel night even if bookings continue to rise. Our recent comparison of Booking's profitability with Airbnb's faster-growing, differentiated supply shows why inventory, distribution and margins deserve to be considered together.
Seeking Alpha's data values Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) at 17.76 times trailing GAAP earnings and 15.31 times forward GAAP earnings; forward non-GAAP P/E is 15.37. That non-GAAP forward multiple is roughly 36% below the five-year average of 24.16, although only modestly above the sector median of 14.84. The consensus projects EPS growth of 14.59% in 2026, 18.41% in 2027, and 16.41% in 2028, a trajectory capable of reducing the prospective P/E over time if achieved.
Cash flow complicates that apparently favorable reading. The second-quarter earnings call reported $3.6 billion of free cash flow, and the company repurchased $7.4 billion of shares in the first half. But merchant bookings allow travelers' money to arrive before Booking pays accommodation providers or processes refunds. Consequently, operating cash flow can be supported by customer-related liabilities that are not distributable earnings. Our closer look at Booking's traveler advances and how much cash shareholders can actually keep addresses that important distinction.
The capital structure also deserves attention: $20.92 billion of debt sits against $17.21 billion of cash, representing approximately $3.71 billion of net debt. The balance sheet is not an immediate sign of distress, but the market's earnings multiple needs to be read alongside buybacks, working capital, and the future cost of defending customer acquisition.
Travel Weakness Makes the Timing Less Forgiving
The operating backdrop offers limited room for complacency. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) lowered its full-year gross-bookings growth expectation in August to high single digits from high single digits to low double digits, citing pressure on international travel, particularly linked to the Middle East conflict. On October 7, Wells Fargo reduced its target to $190 from $220, Equal Weight, citing long-haul weakness and AI risks. Cantor Fitzgerald moved to $170 from $220 on October 12, Neutral, while Morgan Stanley had initiated at Overweight with a $230 target in September, emphasizing supply scale as a competitive advantage.
Hedge fund ownership slipped to 92 from 95 between Q1 and Q2 2026, while shares sold short rose to 22.62 million from 20.15 million between August 31 and September 30, or 3.02% of float. These are positioning snapshots, not proof that investors have reached a verdict on Muse. The next evidence will come from direct booking trends, marketing efficiency, room-night growth, and whether Vayo or Lola can preserve Booking's transaction economics. For a useful contrast, why Airbnb's expansion may command a higher growth multiple examines a different kind of travel-platform exposure.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of BKNG as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.

It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
Furthermore, the different grades of the Zacks Rank are applied proportionately across all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide earnings estimates for the current year. In other words, at all times, this tool maintains a balance among the five ranks it assigns.
There is also a key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank when it comes to freshness. When you look at the ABR, it may not be up-to-date. Nonetheless, since brokerage analysts constantly revise their earnings estimates to reflect changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in predicting future stock prices.

text: Booking Holdings Launches Vayo With Planned $100 Million Investment In AI Personal Travel Agent Booking Holdings has launched Vayo, a new AI-powered personal travel agent, and plans to invest up to $100 million as it explores a more personalized approach to trip planning and management. Vayo is launching in private beta with a waitlist open to travelers. The planned investment depends on continued product development and market conditions. The company is designed to manage an entire trip rather than operate as a general-purpose chatbot or assistant focused on individual tasks. Vayo can bring together existing travel reservations from a user’s inbox, organize trip details, identify missing components, and monitor prices. Because reservations are connected within a single itinerary, the platform is also designed to understand how changes to one part of a trip can affect others. For example, a flight delay could trigger warnings about a late hotel check-in or a dinner reservation that may need to be changed. The company is part of Booking Holdings, whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable. Vayo is being designed to work across Booking Holdings brands as well as reservations made through competing travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels. Vayo’s initial private beta will provide free, invite-only access focused primarily on frequent travelers. The company said the beta period will be used to gather feedback and refine the product before a broader rollout. Vayo will access only travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips rather than the rest of a user’s inbox. Future product plans include direct booking capabilities, a native mobile application, collaborative trip planning with travel companions, and additional assistance once travelers are already on their trips. Booking Holdings is positioning Vayo as an experiment in how AI can move beyond answering travel questions toward proactively managing the interconnected parts of a trip. The company believes personalized travel agents could anticipate user needs based on previous behavior, existing reservations, and trip context. Vayo is led by CEO and co-founder Mike Fridgen. Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said the company is exploring how AI can reduce the amount of planning and coordination work that still falls on travelers.
